Pool and lanai turf for Winter Garden homes

A screened lanai backing Stoneybrook West's course pulls double duty, blocking golf balls along with bugs, and pool-area turf built into one prices at $8–$18 a square foot as of September 2026, typically $10–$16. An older, uncaged pool near Plant Street takes the Florida sun directly, with nothing standing in the way.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say a Stoneybrook West home is adding 500 sq ft of turf inside its screened lanai

Say a Stoneybrook West home backing the course is adding 500 sq ft of turf inside its screened lanai, wrapped around a pool deck that's stayed mostly bare since sod never held up in the shade the cage throws. At the $10–$16 per sq ft range this kind of project typically runs, the job prices between $5,000 and $8,000, with the total landing higher when the perimeter has to be glued to the slab rather than nailed into open ground.

A drainage underlay goes in first everywhere the turf meets concrete, since the cage's frame blocks a share of the rain the fairway beyond it still gets in full. None of that changes because the lot backs a golf course rather than a plain backyard; the build itself is the same either way.

Turf against a fairway-facing pool cage

A lanai that backs Stoneybrook West's course does double duty: the screen keeps insects out the way any pool cage does, and it also stops an errant golf ball from reaching the pool or the turf around it, which is one more reason these enclosures rarely come down even as they age. Turf built into that kind of enclosure still needs a drainage underlay everywhere it meets the concrete deck, since the frame blocks a share of the rain a fairway-facing yard would otherwise get in full.

Glue-down edges against the slab outperform a nailed perimeter inside any screened enclosure, golf-course-facing or not.

Why glued turf follows a different spec sheet than staked turf

A backing glued to a Winter Garden lanai floor's concrete slab answers to a different manufacturer's adhesive and underlay specification than the same backing would if it were seamed over a soil-based rock border, since bonding to concrete calls for a different adhesive chemistry than bonding turf edges to each other over rock. Following the glued-application spec sheet matters for warranty coverage on that portion of the job specifically, separate from whatever spec applies to an open border on the same property. A single property can have two correctly installed sections built to two entirely different sets of manufacturer instructions.

Older Winter Garden pools built before the cage era

Pools near Plant Street's oldest blocks, put in well before Stoneybrook West or any other cage-first subdivision existed, usually never got a screen enclosure at all, since that wasn't standard practice on a Winter Garden lot that early. An open deck like that takes the sun directly, all day, in a way a caged lanai across town never does, which drives surface heat close to the upper end of what installers see in full Florida sun, worth planning for with a lighter or cooling infill right at the coping.

This article covers infill choices that hold up well against an uncovered pool's coping specifically.

Why washed rock matters most where concrete meets soil

Rainfall that hits a pool deck's concrete has nowhere to go but sideways, onto whatever soil border sits at the cage's edge, so a Winter Garden lot's washed, open-graded crushed rock does more work at that transition than it does in the middle of an open lawn. Unwashed fill would let fines settle and bind right where the extra volume arrives first, turning a narrow strip into the one part of the yard that stays soggy after every storm. The state's rule that subgrade material be washed before installation exists for exactly this kind of concentrated flow, not just ordinary rain falling evenly across a yard.

The slight dip that can form around a screen cage footer

A screen cage's concrete footers and the surrounding Winter Garden deck border's rock-and-turf base can settle at slightly different rates over a season or two, since one sits on its own small concrete pad and the other on compacted rock over native sand, and that difference sometimes shows up as a faint dip or ridge ringing each footer. It's rarely a structural issue with either the cage or the turf, just two systems settling independently, but it's worth checking during a routine perimeter walk since a growing gap at a footer can eventually catch a bare foot or trap water in a small ring.

Keeping crew staging off a marked septic lid during a multi-day build

Once a Winter Garden property's septic lid location is flagged before a pool-area turf project starts, keeping material pallets, equipment, and foot traffic off that exact spot for the rest of a multi-day build matters as much as designing the border around it in the first place. A lid that was correctly avoided in the final layout can still end up buried under staged rock or turf rolls left sitting on it overnight if nobody on site remembers where it is. A visible stake or cone marking the spot through the whole job keeps the plan intact from the first day to the last.

Two reasons to rinse a pool border more than once a week in summer

Hosing down turf along a Winter Garden pool deck does two jobs at once: it clears chlorine or salt splash and pollen before either dries into the fibers, and it drops surface temperature 30 to 50 degrees ahead of an afternoon swim. Rainy-season storms between June and September handle some of that rinsing on their own, but the dry stretches on either side of summer leave splash as the only source of moisture on the turf, so a hose rinse earns its place in the routine year-round rather than just during the hottest weeks. Keeping shock and acid containers off the turf's edge avoids undoing the rinse entirely.

A pool deck's turf and the 10-ft setback on a Black Lake lot

A handful of Black Lake-facing lots put the pool deck close enough to the shoreline that the state's 10-foot waterbody setback becomes the real limit on how far a turf border can run toward the water, not the cage's own footprint. Where a seawall already separates the yard from the lake, that setback doesn't apply the same way; where it's just a natural bank, the 10 feet gets measured before the deck's turf border is ever drawn.

That's a different constraint than the drainage question a screened cage raises, and it's worth settling before ordering material for a lakefront pool project specifically.

Questions people ask

Does turf inside a Winter Garden pool cage need a different base than an open yard?

Only where the two surfaces meet. Concrete gets a drainage underlay and a glued perimeter; open ground gets a compacted rock base and a nailed or bordered edge instead. Everywhere else inside the cage, the build matches a plain lawn.

Is pool-area turf hotter in an older, uncovered Winter Garden pool than a caged one?

Usually, since a screen blocks a meaningful share of direct sun that an open deck takes all day long. A cooling or lighter-colored infill closes part of that gap, and a hose rinse closes the rest within minutes.

Do I need a permit for turf around a pool in Winter Garden?

Turf on its own doesn't trigger anything beyond the city's usual synthetic-turf permitting, though changing the cage structure itself is a separate matter. Check with the Building Division at 407-877-5136 if the scope covers both.
